This annual output, though modest compared to some tropical thrushes, allows sufficient investment in each nestling. Field studies measuring body mass at the point of hatching have recorded a neonatal wet weight of approximately 3.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.5 grams], placing the species within the expected range for a passerine of its adult body size. This initial mass is sustained entirely by parental provisioning, as newly hatched young are altricial and entirely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and nutrition during the first days post-hatching.

This accelerated growth trajectory is typical of altricial passerines and is sustained by the high-frequency provisioning efforts of both parents, who together may deliver food items to the nest dozens of times per day.

This age at fledging is relatively short compared to some other thrush species of similar body mass, possibly reflecting selection pressures from nest predation in the species' preferred woodland edge and hedgerow habitats. After leaving the nest, fledglings remain dependent on parental care for an additional period, during which they refine their foraging skills and gradually attain nutritional independence. The relatively early fledging age is a common pattern among open-nesting passerines, balancing the benefits of reduced nest exposure against the increased vulnerability of flight-inexperienced young on the ground.

The maximum lifespan of the Song Thrush has been documented through long-term ringing studies across Europe. Under natural conditions, the oldest recorded individuals reach approximately 17.5 years [am = approximately 17.5 years] when measured at the species' typical active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], representing an exceptional longevity for a passerine of this body size. This combination of a relatively long potential lifespan and a moderate body mass suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival over high annual fecundity. Individuals that survive the high mortality risks of their first winter can potentially contribute to reproduction over many breeding seasons, thereby offsetting the relatively modest annual reproductive output with a longer reproductive window.
